opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the things I've seen over and over is that when a business looks at a workflow, say, processing an invoice, onboarding a customer, or doing a compliance review, it's tempting to think, "Let's just hand the whole thing to an agent end to end." But real business processes are made up of lots of small steps, and the hard part is deciding *how* to break them down and *where* the AI is reliable enough to act on its own.

That decomposition itself takes a lot of judgment. You need someone who understands the business well enough to say, "This step, extracting fields from a document, the AI can do at 99% accuracy, so let it run. But this other step, deciding whether to approve an exception or flag a vendor, has real consequences if it's wrong, so let's put a human in the loop there, at least for now."

And then there's the iterative piece. When we build agentic workflows, the systems don't work perfectly out of the gate. You have to look at the outputs, do error analysis, and figure out which step in a ten-step pipeline is causing the problems. Is it the retrieval? The reasoning step? The tool call? Teams that are really good at this have developed a kind of disciplined intuition: they build evals, look at traces, and make good calls about where to focus. That's still very much a human skill, and frankly it's one of the biggest predictors I see of whether a team succeeds.

And finally, there's accountability. In many businesses, someone has to own the decision, especially in regulated areas or customer-facing ones. Agents can do a huge amount of the work, and I think the fraction they handle will keep going up. But knowing when to trust the system, when to escalate, and how to design the workflow so that humans spend their time on the highest-value judgment calls is what separates deployments that create real value from ones that stall out in a demo.

r001.rationale: The response says business knowledge is needed to decide which steps can run autonomously and which consequential decisions need human review, tying acceptable error risk to the specific business process.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So when I look at how businesses actually implement agentic workflows, the first thing I notice is that the hard part is almost never the model. The hard part is figuring out what the workflow should be in the first place.

Take something like processing a customer complaint, or reviewing a contract, or handling a reimbursement request. If you ask someone to describe how that gets done, they'll give you a clean five-step story. But when you sit down and watch them do it, you find there are all these little judgment calls. "Oh, if the customer has been with us more than three years, I'd escalate this one." "Oh, this vendor is tricky, I always double-check their invoices." None of that is written down anywhere. It lives in people's heads.

So when you build a multi-step agent, somebody has to decompose that messy process into discrete steps the agent can execute, and decide what goes in each step. That decomposition is a human judgment task. I don't think you can hand it entirely to the model, because the model doesn't know what your business cares about, what's acceptable risk, or which edge cases actually matter versus which ones are harmless.

The second place human judgment is essential is evaluation. In a multi-step workflow, when something goes wrong at the end, you have to trace back and figure out which step was responsible. Was it the retrieval? Was it the reasoning in step three? Was it a bad tool call? Building good evals for each step, and deciding what "good enough" means for each of them, is genuinely hard, and it requires someone who understands the domain. I spend a lot of time telling teams that their eval process is the real bottleneck, not the model.

And then the third piece is deciding where the agent should stop and ask a person. For a lot of business processes, the right design isn't fully autonomous. It's an agent that does the first eighty percent reliably and then routes the ambiguous cases to a human. Deciding where that boundary sits, and how it should move over time as you gain confidence, is a judgment call that depends on the cost of errors in your specific context.

So I'm very bullish on agents. I think they're going to do a huge amount of work. But the teams I see succeeding are the ones that treat the humans as the designers and the quality controllers of the workflow, rather than hoping the model will somehow figure out the business on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says the model cannot know what the business considers acceptable risk and that error costs depend on the specific context.

astra-6.text:
When you build a multi-step agent workflow, you have to decide which steps the AI can do reliably and where a person should review the result. Those decisions depend on the business context. What does a mistake cost? Is it reversible? Is there an exception that requires someone who understands the customer or the organization?

For example, drafting an email and authorizing a payment might both be steps in a workflow, but they warrant very different levels of oversight. And even if each individual step looks pretty good, an error early on can propagate through the rest of the process.

So human judgment matters both in designing the workflow and in handling the cases where the system shouldn't proceed on its own. You can automate more as you gather evidence that it works reliably, but you need people to establish what success means and what risks are acceptable.

r001.rationale: The response says decisions about which steps need human review depend on business context, including the cost and reversibility of mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
When you build an agentic workflow, you’re breaking a task into multiple steps, and there are judgment calls about where to use AI, what tools to give it, and when to ask a person for help. A business process may have exceptions or requirements that aren’t captured in the written instructions. Someone has to decide what a good outcome actually looks like and what mistakes are acceptable.

For example, an agent might draft a response to a customer, look up an order, and recommend a refund. But issuing that refund could require approval, depending on the amount or the circumstances. The engineering challenge is to give the system useful autonomy while putting human review at the points where it matters. Then you evaluate the whole workflow, look at where it fails, and improve those steps.

r001.rationale: The response says acceptable mistakes depend on a business process’s exceptions and requirements, and that refund approval can depend on the amount or circumstances, communicating that acceptability requires business-specific context.
